section_summary: This section finishes a survey of voting preferences among married couples in three Japanese communities, then presents a despatch and memorandum on government, education, democracy, and Military Government in Kyushu. It also contains a damaged airgram reporting Soviet press commentary, a conversation with former ambassador Kensuke Horinouchi, an incoming telegram cover sheet, and an airgram about a fatal incident involving Japan Communist Party concerns.

subfiles.title: Survey of married couples’ electoral preferences, with publication colophon
subfiles.about: Survey results compare husbands’ and wives’ voting preferences and knowledge of one another’s choices in three communities.
subfiles.summary: The excerpt gives survey dates, questions, and tabulated responses for 300 couples in Yamato-chō, Ōme, and Yuzurihara. It concludes that husbands generally influenced wives’ party choices more than the reverse. A Japanese colophon records publication on May 25, 1948.

subfiles.title: Observations Concerning Government, Democracy and Education, and Military Government in Kyushu
subfiles.from: W. J. Sebald, United States Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: Sebald forwards Lawrence’s observations from a visit to four Kyushu prefectures.
subfiles.summary: Sebald highlights weak public engagement in local government, the need for sustained democratic education and greater school funding, and Japanese interest in American publications and overseas study. He recommends curbing Military Government’s direction of everyday Japanese affairs to encourage Japanese officials’ initiative.

subfiles.title: Observations Concerning Government, Democracy and Education, and Military Government in Kyushu
subfiles.to: Office of the Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: Lawrence reports interviews and observations from his Kyushu orientation visit.
subfiles.summary: Lawrence describes limited public understanding of democratic government, inefficient and overlapping offices, and uncertainty about the Occupation’s authority. Educators report inadequate funding, housing, salaries, and supplies, while students and professionals seek access to American study and publications. He also records Japanese reactions to American films and troops. Military Government personnel vary in training and frequently direct Japanese administrative work; Lawrence argues that this dependence should be reduced.

subfiles.title: Soviet press commentary on Japan, trade unions, and reconstruction plans
subfiles.about: The airgram relays Soviet press criticism of American and Japanese policies toward Japan.
subfiles.summary: The damaged text reproduces commentary alleging plans for a loan to Japan and suppression of trade unions under the Ashida government. It praises Communist influence in Japanese labor organizations and criticizes American proposals for Japan’s economic reconstruction.

subfiles.title: Conversation with former ambassador Kensuke Horinouchi
subfiles.from: H. M. Benninghoff, Office of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.about: Horinouchi discusses diplomatic training, the Japanese press, and public attitudes after the war.
subfiles.summary: Horinouchi says he teaches prospective Japanese foreign service officers about democratic processes. He describes the press as having swung from left to right, observes some renewed public hope tied to trade and possible American aid, and expresses concern about declining everyday morality.

subfiles.title: Incoming telegram record copy
subfiles.about: A restricted incoming telegram cover records receipt and filing information.
subfiles.summary: Cover sheet only; the telegram’s message text is absent.

subfiles.title: Airgram on a fatal incident and Communist Party concerns
subfiles.from: United States Political Adviser for Japan, Tokyo
subfiles.about: The airgram reports a fatal apparent hit-and-run incident and concern about its investigation.
subfiles.summary: An apparent hit-and-run death in Tokyo prompts an investigation. Communist leader Nosaka Sanzō criticizes police efforts and threatens to seek further Allied investigation.
